✅ NOT A WOKE TRAP

NOT A WOKE TRAP. The anti-fascist themes are the continuation of a storyline established across two full seasons of television. Tim Roth's fascist villain Beckett is a direct successor to Sam Claflin's Oswald Mosley. There is nothing smuggled in. The marketing, the trailers, and every interview with Steven Knight and Cillian Murphy have been transparent about the WWII setting and the fascist antagonist. Conservative viewers who enjoyed Seasons 5 and 6 will find familiar territory here.

Overall Perspective

Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man is a film that knows exactly what it is and refuses to apologize for it. It is a masculine, violent, morally complex crime drama about a deeply flawed man who comes out of hiding to save his son, fight fascists, and protect his family during Britain's darkest hour. In 2026, that sentence alone makes it notable.

The setup is elegant. It is 1940. Birmingham is being carpet-bombed by the Luftwaffe. Tommy Shelby has been living in monastic isolation, haunted by the ghosts of everyone he has lost and everyone he has killed. His illegitimate son Duke, now played by Barry Keoghan, has taken over the Peaky Blinders and is running the operation with the reckless brutality of a man who never had a father to teach him restraint. Tim Roth's Beckett, Treasurer of the British Union of Fascists, is whispering in Duke's ear about treason and collaboration with Germany. Ada Shelby, now an MP, tells Tommy: 'Your gypsy son is running the Peaky Blinders like it is 1919 all over again.' Tommy must return to save his son, confront his legacy, and decide whether to burn it all down or reclaim what he built.

This is a story built on foundations that conservative audiences will recognize immediately. Fatherhood. Legacy. Duty. Patriotism against fascism. The consequences of abandoning your responsibilities. Tommy Shelby is not a good man - the series has never pretended otherwise - but he is a man who, when the stakes are real, chooses family and country over self-preservation. That moral architecture has been the spine of Peaky Blinders since Season 1, and the film appears to honor it completely.

Steven Knight wrote the screenplay solo, drawing on his own family's experience of the Birmingham Blitz. His mother lived through those bombings. His father worked in Digbeth, the neighborhood where the film was shot at Knight's own purpose-built studio. This is not a Hollywood committee product. It is one writer's vision, rooted in personal history and regional identity, brought to screen by a director (Tom Harper) who helped establish the show's visual language in Season 1.

The anti-fascist theme deserves careful analysis because it is the element most likely to draw culture-war attention. Peaky Blinders has been explicitly anti-fascist since Season 5 introduced Oswald Mosley (Sam Claflin) as the primary antagonist. The show depicted the British Union of Fascists as a genuine domestic threat - which historically, they were. The Immortal Man continues this by introducing Beckett, a BUF Treasurer who attempts to recruit Duke into treason. This is not modern progressive 'everyone I disagree with is a fascist' framing. This is 1940 Britain. The fascists are actual fascists allied with actual Nazis during an actual world war. The anti-fascism here is the same anti-fascism that Churchill, Eisenhower, and every Allied soldier embodied. It is historically grounded patriotism, not contemporary political allegory.

Some progressive commentators have tried to claim Peaky Blinders as an anti-capitalist, anti-masculine text. A Medium article described it as depicting 'the failure of hegemonic-neoliberal masculinity.' One critic in 2022 called Tommy Shelby a 'cultural symbol for capitalist and virilistic mentality.' These readings exist but they are academic impositions on a text that has always celebrated masculine competence, loyalty, and cunning even while acknowledging their costs. Tommy Shelby became a global male icon not because viewers missed the point, but because the show genuinely admires what it depicts while honestly showing the price.

Cillian Murphy's stated philosophy further reinforces the film's entertainment-first posture. In a Telegraph interview released just yesterday, Murphy said: 'The last thing I want to be involved in is preachy or dogmatic work because films should never tell you how to feel. They should just ask questions. This should be an entertaining action film with a big heart.' When your lead actor and producer explicitly rejects preachiness in the current Hollywood climate, that is worth noting.

The cast is exceptional. Murphy returns to his signature role after winning an Oscar for Oppenheimer. Keoghan brings feral charisma. Ferguson adds mystery and supernatural weight. Roth is a masterclass in quiet menace. Graham provides working-class authenticity. Rundle grounds the family drama. The production shot practically at Knight's Digbeth Loc. Studios with real explosions and period cars rather than relying on green screen. Roth praised the production: 'It properly feels like an old Second World War movie. It had ambition.'

The woke content is minimal and largely consists of elements that are inherent to the source material rather than imposed upon it. Rebecca Ferguson's Kaulo represents the show's longstanding engagement with powerful female characters and Romani mysticism. Ada Shelby being an MP reflects her character arc across six seasons of television - she was always the politically ambitious Shelby. The anti-fascist framing is historically accurate rather than allegorical. There is no race-swapping, no gender-swapping, no DEI casting, and no visible demographic engineering.

The traditional content is substantial. Father-son redemption. Patriotic duty during wartime. Masculine competence and sacrifice. Family loyalty as the highest value. A working-class hero who built an empire through cunning and violence but ultimately fights for something bigger than himself. The portrayal of fascism as a genuine evil to be physically confronted rather than merely debated. The entire dramatic engine runs on values that conservative audiences hold dear.

This is a pre-release assessment based on trailers, interviews, set visits, and the established patterns of the Peaky Blinders franchise. The full review will be updated after the Netflix premiere on March 20, 2026. Based on everything available, Peaky Blinders: The Immortal Man appears to be that increasingly rare thing: a prestige entertainment that respects its audience, trusts its material, and refuses to lecture.

Creative Team Deep Dive

Director: Tom Harper

NEUTRAL. Harper grew up in a Quaker family and credits Quakerism with shaping his attitudes toward equality and fairness, but his filmography shows no consistent ideological pattern. Wild Rose (2018) is a working-class uplift story about a single mother pursuing her country music dream. The Aeronauts (2019) is a period adventure. War and Peace (2016) is a faithful Tolstoy adaptation. He directed the back half of Peaky Blinders Season 1, establishing the show's visual language alongside cinematographer George Steel. His return to the franchise is a creative homecoming, not an ideological appointment.

British film and television director born January 7, 1980. Grew up in a Quaker household. Studied at the National Film and Television School. His early career included BBC television work before breaking through with Wild Rose, which earned Jessie Buckley a BAFTA nomination. The Aeronauts starred Eddie Redmayne and Felicity Jones. Harper directed episodes of Peaky Blinders Season 1 and returns to close the saga alongside cinematographer George Steel, who also shot Season 1. Murphy specifically requested Harper for the film, citing trust and their shared understanding of the Peaky Blinders visual world.

Writer: Steven Knight

Birmingham-born writer, producer, and creator of Peaky Blinders. Knight is one of British television's most prolific and commercially successful writers. He co-created Who Wants to Be a Millionaire?, wrote the screenplays for Dirty Pretty Things (2002), Eastern Promises (2007), Locke (2013), Spencer (2021), and See (Apple TV+). He created the series Taboo with Tom Hardy and Chips Hardy. Knight drew on his own family history for Peaky Blinders - his father worked in Digbeth, Birmingham, shoeing police horses, and his mother lived through the Birmingham Blitz that forms the backdrop of this film. He built Digbeth Loc. Studios in Birmingham specifically to house this production. Knight has written all 36 hours of Peaky Blinders television and the film screenplay solo. His storytelling sensibility is working-class, masculine, and rooted in the specific texture of Birmingham's industrial history. He has described the series as being about 'what happens when rough men gain power.'

Adult Viewer Insight

Conservative adults should approach this with confidence. Peaky Blinders has always been one of the few prestige dramas that genuinely respects masculine archetypes, working-class identity, and family loyalty while honestly depicting their costs. The WWII anti-fascist framing is historically patriotic, not politically allegorical. Cillian Murphy's explicit rejection of preachy filmmaking in interviews is a positive signal. The creative team is the same writer (Knight) and director (Harper from Season 1) who built the franchise. Netflix distribution means you can watch it at home on March 20 if you prefer not to do the limited theatrical run on March 6. This is likely to be one of the most satisfying prestige films of early 2026 for conservative audiences.

Parental Guidance

Expected R rating for violence, language, and mature content. Recommended age: 16 and up. This is a continuation of a TV series rated TV-MA for intense violence, strong language, sexual content, and drug/alcohol use. The film reportedly features large-scale WWII bombing sequences, gang violence, and the morally complex world the series is known for. Not appropriate for children or young teenagers. Older teenagers (16+) who have watched the series will find familiar territory. The father-son conflict, the anti-fascist themes, and the consequences of abandoning family are all discussion-worthy topics for mature viewers. No woke content that would surprise or blindside parents familiar with the show.
